You use wish, plus the past form of the verb or the past participle of the verb to talk about imaginary situations in the past, present or future.
Wishes and sentences in the second and third conditional infer that what you want is probably not possible, or for some reason impossible and that you regret what happened in the past.

images.text:
Vanessa: You must have been shocked!
Sally: Well, that's not the worst of it. When I went to my branch they told me that someone has been trying to move my assets around. Luckily they were missing some information. I must have been hacked!
Vanessa: I wish people weren't so abominable!
Sally: Ditto! I'm stumped though. They must have got my name and info all online. How did they do it?

Vanessa: I wish the world weren't so cruel. Someone must have found out that you won the lottery.
Sally: That's for sure. I wish I hadn't told anyone but you and Peter! I knew this would come back to haunt me.
Vanessa: It might have been someone at the party in the restaurant. Remember, you bought everyone a meal and announced that you had won?
Sally: It was a celebration. I was happy! Maybe it was that guy who was all creepy and standing in the corner with that evil grin. Now I wish I had been more cautious. I didn't realize this could happen.

Vanessa: Well, at least you don't have to pay that Visa bill and your money is safe. You should be relieved about that. I just wish people who do this sort of thing would get caught and pay for it.
Sally: I wish I didn't feel violated.
Vanessa: Everything is going to be okay. Let's have some tea and homemade cookies.
Sally: Yes! You are the best, V!
